chapter_text:
CHAPTER 19 - DISPERSION AND SCATTERING OF LIGHT

Introduction

When a narrow beam of sunlight passes through a glass prism it spreads out into a band of colours ranging from red at one edge to violet at the other. This splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called DISPERSION, and the coloured band is the SPECTRUM. Isaac Newton first showed (around 1666) that white light is not a simple, pure colour but a mixture of many colours, and that a prism merely separates them. In this chapter we study why dispersion happens, how it is measured through dispersive power, the different kinds of spectra that light sources produce, how rainbows are formed, and how the SCATTERING of light by small particles explains the blue of the sky, the red of the setting Sun, and the choice of red for danger signals.

19.1 DISPERSION OF WHITE LIGHT BY A PRISM

When white light enters a glass prism, each colour bends (refracts) by a different amount. Violet light bends the most and red light bends the least; the other colours lie in between. The colours in order, from least to most deviated, are Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet - remembered by the word VIBGYOR read from violet to red. The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray is the angle of deviation. Because violet is deviated most, delta_violet > delta_red.

CAUSE OF DISPERSION. The refractive index n of a transparent medium is not a single fixed number; it depends on the wavelength (colour) of the light passing through it. For ordinary glass, n is larger for short wavelengths (violet) and smaller for long wavelengths (red): n_violet > n_red. Since the deviation produced by a thin prism is delta = (n - 1) A, where A is the refracting angle of the prism, a larger n gives a larger deviation. Violet, having the highest n, is deviated most; red, having the lowest n, is deviated least. In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed c and so there is no dispersion in vacuum - dispersion is a property of the material medium, not of light itself. This is why a spectrum forms in glass or water but not in empty space.

19.2 ANGULAR DISPERSION AND DISPERSIVE POWER

For a thin prism the deviation of any colour is delta = (n - 1) A. The ANGULAR DISPERSION is the difference in deviation between the two extreme colours (violet and red):
  angular dispersion = delta_violet - delta_red = (n_violet - n_red) A.
It measures the total angular spread of the spectrum produced by the prism.

The DISPERSIVE POWER (omega) of the prism material is defined as the ratio of the angular dispersion to the mean deviation. Taking yellow as the mean colour,
  omega = (delta_violet - delta_red) / delta_yellow = (n_violet - n_red) / (n_yellow - 1).
Dispersive power is a pure number (no units) and depends ONLY on the material of the prism, not on its refracting angle A. A material with a large omega spreads the colours widely for a given mean deviation. Flint glass has a higher dispersive power than crown glass, which is why the two are combined in achromatic lens systems: a crown prism and a flint prism can be arranged so that their dispersions cancel while a net deviation remains (an achromatic combination), or so that deviations cancel while dispersion remains (a direct-vision prism).

Worked example: For a prism, n_violet = 1.532, n_red = 1.514, and n_yellow = 1.523. Then omega = (1.532 - 1.514) / (1.523 - 1) = 0.018 / 0.523 = 0.0344. If the refracting angle is A = 5 degrees, the angular dispersion = (n_violet - n_red) A = 0.018 x 5 = 0.09 degrees.

19.3 PURE AND IMPURE SPECTRUM

A PURE SPECTRUM is one in which the colours do not overlap - each colour occupies a distinct position and the lines are sharp. An IMPURE SPECTRUM is one in which neighbouring colours overlap so the band looks smeared. To obtain a pure spectrum four conditions must be met: (i) a narrow slit must be used as the source, (ii) a lens must render the light from the slit parallel before it strikes the prism (a collimator), (iii) the prism must be set in the position of minimum deviation, and (iv) a second lens must focus each parallel emergent beam to a sharp image on the screen. A spectrometer is the instrument that satisfies all these conditions.

19.4 TYPES OF SPECTRA

Spectra are broadly of two kinds: EMISSION spectra (produced by light coming directly from a source) and ABSORPTION spectra (produced when white light passes through a medium that removes certain wavelengths).

EMISSION SPECTRA are of three types:
(a) CONTINUOUS spectrum - an unbroken band containing all wavelengths, with one colour merging into the next. Hot glowing solids, liquids, and highly compressed hot gases give continuous spectra. Examples: the filament of an electric bulb, molten metal, the Sun's photosphere.
(b) LINE spectrum - a set of sharp, bright, isolated lines on a dark background, each line a definite wavelength. Excited atoms of a gas at low pressure (for example sodium vapour, hydrogen, neon, or mercury in a discharge tube) give line spectra. Every element has its own characteristic set of lines, so a line spectrum is a 'fingerprint' that identifies the element.
(c) BAND spectrum - groups of very closely spaced lines that appear as bright bands, each band sharp at one edge and fading at the other. Band spectra are emitted by excited MOLECULES (not single atoms), for example nitrogen or carbon dioxide.

ABSORPTION SPECTRA. When white light with a continuous spectrum passes through a cooler gas or vapour, the gas absorbs exactly those wavelengths that it would emit if it were hot. The result is a continuous spectrum crossed by DARK LINES at the missing wavelengths. This is an absorption (or dark-line) spectrum. A famous example is the solar spectrum: sunlight from the hot photosphere is a continuous spectrum, but the cooler gases of the Sun's outer atmosphere absorb certain wavelengths, producing thousands of dark lines. These are the FRAUNHOFER LINES, first mapped by Joseph von Fraunhofer. By matching the dark lines with the bright lines of known elements, astronomers identify the elements present in the Sun and stars (this is how helium was first discovered - in the Sun).

THE SPECTROMETER (in brief). A spectrometer has three main parts: a COLLIMATOR (a slit plus a lens that produces a parallel beam), a PRISM table on which the prism is mounted, and a TELESCOPE that gathers the emergent parallel rays and forms a sharp spectrum. By rotating the telescope on a graduated circular scale, the angle of each spectral line can be measured, allowing the refractive index and dispersive power of the prism to be found and the wavelengths of spectral lines to be studied.

19.5 RECOMBINATION OF THE SPECTRUM

Newton also showed that dispersion is reversible: the colours can be recombined into white light. If a second, identical but inverted prism is placed after the first, it bends the colours back together and white light emerges. Alternatively, a NEWTON'S DISC - a circular disc painted with the seven VIBGYOR colours in sectors - appears whitish (greyish white) when spun rapidly, because the eye cannot resolve the individual colours and blends them together on the retina. Both experiments confirm that white light is simply the combination of the seven colours.

19.6 THE RAINBOW

A rainbow is a large-scale natural spectrum formed by sunlight falling on raindrops. Two processes act inside each drop: REFRACTION (which disperses the colours because water, like glass, has a wavelength-dependent refractive index) and TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (which turns the light back towards the observer).

PRIMARY RAINBOW. Sunlight enters the top of a raindrop, is refracted and dispersed, undergoes ONE total internal reflection at the back of the drop, and is refracted again as it leaves. The light emerges at an angle of about 40 to 42 degrees to the incoming sunlight. In the primary bow RED appears on the OUTER (top) edge and VIOLET on the INNER (bottom) edge. The observer must stand with the Sun BEHIND them, looking towards the rain.

SECONDARY RAINBOW. When light undergoes TWO total internal reflections inside the drop before emerging, a fainter secondary bow appears at about 50 to 54 degrees, outside the primary bow. Because of the extra reflection the colour order is REVERSED - red is on the inner edge and violet on the outer edge. The secondary bow is fainter because some light is lost at each reflection.

19.7 SCATTERING OF LIGHT

When light travels through a medium containing small particles - dust, smoke, water droplets, or even the molecules of air - part of the light is redirected in all directions. This redirection is SCATTERING. The amount of scattering depends strongly on the size of the particles relative to the wavelength of light and on the wavelength itself.

RAYLEIGH'S LAW OF SCATTERING. Lord Rayleigh showed that when the scattering particles are much SMALLER than the wavelength of light, the intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength:
  I is proportional to 1 / lambda^4.
This means short wavelengths are scattered far more strongly than long wavelengths. Violet and blue light (short lambda) are scattered much more than red light (long lambda). For example, since the wavelength of red (about 700 nm) is roughly twice that of violet (about 400 nm), the ratio of scattered intensities is about (700/400)^4, so violet is scattered several times more strongly than red. Rayleigh scattering applies only to particles much smaller than lambda; for larger particles the scattering becomes nearly independent of wavelength.

19.8 EVERYDAY PHENOMENA EXPLAINED BY SCATTERING

BLUE COLOUR OF THE SKY. The molecules of air are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, so Rayleigh's law applies. Sunlight passing through the atmosphere is scattered by air molecules, and because scattering goes as 1/lambda^4, the shorter wavelengths (blue and violet) are scattered far more than the longer ones. The scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions in the sky, so the sky looks blue. (It is not violet, even though violet is scattered slightly more, because sunlight contains less violet and the eye is less sensitive to violet.) On the Moon, which has no atmosphere, there is no scattering and the sky appears black even in daytime.

REDDISH SUN AT SUNRISE AND SUNSET. At sunrise and sunset the Sun is near the horizon, so its light travels a much longer path through the atmosphere than at noon. Along this long path most of the blue and violet light is scattered away sideways, and mainly the longer wavelengths (red and orange) survive to reach the observer directly. Hence the Sun and the surrounding sky look red or orange. At noon the path is shortest, less blue is removed, and the Sun looks white or pale yellow.

WHITE CLOUDS. Clouds are made of relatively LARGE water droplets whose size is comparable to or larger than the wavelengths of visible light. For such large particles Rayleigh's law does not apply; all wavelengths are scattered almost equally (this is large-particle or Mie scattering). Since all colours are scattered by the same amount, the scattered light remains white - so clouds look white.

DANGER SIGNALS ARE RED. Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible range, so by Rayleigh's law it is scattered the LEAST by fog, smoke, and dust particles. Red light therefore penetrates farthest through a hazy atmosphere and can be seen from the greatest distance. That is why red is chosen for stop signals, brake lights, and other danger and warning signs.

TYNDALL EFFECT. When a beam of light passes through a colloid or a medium containing fine suspended particles (such as smoke, fog, or a dusty room lit by a sunbeam), the path of the beam becomes visible because the particles scatter the light sideways towards the eye. This scattering of light by colloidal particles is the TYNDALL EFFECT. It is the reason we can see the beam of a cinema projector or a torch in a smoky room, and it also shows a bluish tinge when the particles are very small, again because short wavelengths scatter most.

SUMMARY

- Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours (VIBGYOR) by a prism; it occurs because the refractive index depends on wavelength, with n_violet > n_red, so violet deviates most and red least.
- For a thin prism, deviation delta = (n - 1) A; angular dispersion = (n_violet - n_red) A; dispersive power omega = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1), a unit-less number depending only on the material.
- A pure spectrum needs a narrow slit, a collimator, minimum-deviation setting, and a focusing lens; a spectrometer provides these.
- Emission spectra are continuous (hot solids/liquids/dense gases), line (excited atoms - element fingerprints), or band (excited molecules); absorption spectra show dark lines (Fraunhofer lines in the solar spectrum).
- Dispersion is reversible: an inverted prism or a spinning Newton's disc recombines the colours into white.
- A rainbow forms by refraction (dispersion) plus total internal reflection in raindrops: primary bow at about 40-42 degrees (red outside, one reflection); secondary bow at about 50-54 degrees (red inside, two reflections).
- Scattering redistributes light; Rayleigh's law (I proportional to 1/lambda^4) holds for particles much smaller than lambda, so blue scatters far more than red.
- Scattering explains the blue sky, the red Sun at sunrise/sunset, white clouds (large droplets scatter all colours equally), red danger signals (least scattered, travel farthest), and the Tyndall effect.

chapter_summary.title: Dispersion and Scattering of Light - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter explains how a prism splits white light into the VIBGYOR spectrum (dispersion), how dispersive power measures the spread, the kinds of spectra sources emit, how rainbows form, and how the scattering of light (Rayleigh's law) accounts for the blue sky, red sunsets, white clouds and red danger signals.

sections.heading: Dispersion by a prism
bullets: White light passing through a prism spreads into a spectrum of colours - Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (VIBGYOR).
Dispersion happens because the refractive index n of the glass depends on the wavelength: n is largest for violet and smallest for red, so n_violet > n_red.
For a thin prism each colour deviates by delta = (n-1)A; violet has the largest n so it is deviated most, red the least.
Dispersion occurs in a material medium but not in vacuum, where all colours travel at the same speed c.

sections.heading: Angular dispersion and dispersive power
bullets: Angular dispersion is the angular spread between the extreme colours: (delta_violet - delta_red) = (n_violet - n_red)A.
Dispersive power omega = (delta_violet - delta_red)/delta_yellow = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1).
omega is a pure number that depends only on the material of the prism, not on its refracting angle.
Flint glass has higher dispersive power than crown glass; combining the two gives achromatic (deviation without dispersion) or direct-vision (dispersion without deviation) prisms.

sections.heading: Types of spectra
bullets: Emission spectra are of three kinds: continuous (hot solids, liquids, dense gases), line (excited atoms - a fingerprint of the element), and band (excited molecules).
An absorption spectrum is a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines produced when white light passes through a cooler gas.
The dark lines in the solar spectrum are the Fraunhofer lines; matching them to element lines reveals the composition of the Sun and stars.
A pure spectrum (no colour overlap) requires a narrow slit, a collimator, minimum-deviation setting, and a focusing lens - all provided by a spectrometer.

sections.heading: The rainbow
bullets: A rainbow forms when sunlight is refracted, dispersed and totally internally reflected inside raindrops, with the Sun behind the observer.
The primary rainbow (one internal reflection) appears at about 40-42 degrees with red on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge.
The secondary rainbow (two internal reflections) appears at about 50-54 degrees, is fainter, and has the colour order reversed (red inside).
Recombining the colours (an inverted prism or a spinning Newton's disc) gives back white light, showing dispersion is reversible.

sections.heading: Scattering and everyday phenomena
bullets: Rayleigh's law: for particles much smaller than the wavelength, scattered intensity I is proportional to 1/lambda^4, so blue scatters far more than red.
The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths most; the Sun looks red at sunrise/sunset because blue is scattered away over the long atmospheric path.
Clouds look white because their large water droplets scatter all wavelengths almost equally.
Red is used for danger signals because it is scattered least and travels farthest through haze; the Tyndall effect makes a light beam visible in a dusty or colloidal medium.

Rayleigh's law I proportional to 1/lambda^4 holds for particles much smaller than the wavelength, so short wavelengths scatter most.
Scattering explains the blue sky, the red Sun at sunrise/sunset, white clouds (large droplets), red danger signals, and the Tyndall effect.

glossary.definition: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours (VIBGYOR) when it passes through a medium such as a prism.
The band of colours obtained when white light is dispersed; ranges from red to violet.
The seven colours of the spectrum - Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red - in order of decreasing deviation.
The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray after refraction through a prism.
The difference in deviation between the two extreme colours, (n_violet - n_red)A for a thin prism.
The ratio of angular dispersion to mean deviation, omega = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1); a unit-less quantity depending only on the material.
A spectrum in which the colours do not overlap, giving sharp, distinct lines.
An unbroken band of all wavelengths, emitted by hot solids, liquids, or dense gases.
Sharp bright isolated lines emitted by excited atoms of a gas; a characteristic fingerprint of each element.
Groups of closely spaced lines forming bands, emitted by excited molecules.
A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines, formed when white light passes through a cooler gas that absorbs certain wavelengths.
The dark absorption lines in the solar spectrum, caused by absorption in the Sun's cooler outer gases.
The redirection of light in many directions by small particles in a medium.
For particles much smaller than the wavelength, the scattered intensity is proportional to 1/lambda^4.
The scattering of light by colloidal or fine suspended particles, making the path of a light beam visible.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Dispersion and Scattering of Light
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. For numerical problems show your working and give answers to a sensible number of significant figures. Use lambda for wavelength and omega for dispersive power.

questions.question: What is dispersion of light? State why violet light is deviated more than red light by a glass prism.
questions.answer: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its constituent colours (VIBGYOR) when it passes through a prism. It occurs because the refractive index of glass depends on wavelength: n is greater for violet (short lambda) than for red (long lambda), i.e. n_violet > n_red. Since deviation delta = (n-1)A increases with n, violet with the larger n is deviated more than red.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the wavelength dependence of n.

questions.question: Define angular dispersion and dispersive power. On what does dispersive power depend?
questions.answer: Angular dispersion is the angular separation between the two extreme colours: (delta_violet - delta_red) = (n_violet - n_red)A. Dispersive power omega is the ratio of angular dispersion to mean deviation: omega = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1). It is a pure number and depends only on the material of the prism, not on its refracting angle A.
questions.explanation: Both definitions plus material-only dependence.

questions.question: For a prism, n_violet = 1.652, n_red = 1.644 and n_yellow = 1.648. Calculate the dispersive power of the material.
questions.answer: omega = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1) = (1.652 - 1.644)/(1.648 - 1) = 0.008/0.648 = 0.01235. So omega is about 0.0123 (a pure number).
questions.explanation: Direct substitution into omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1).

questions.question: A thin prism of refracting angle 6 degrees has n_violet = 1.532 and n_red = 1.514. Find the angular dispersion produced.
questions.answer: Angular dispersion = (n_violet - n_red)A = (1.532 - 1.514) x 6 = 0.018 x 6 = 0.108 degrees.
questions.explanation: Apply angular dispersion = (n_v - n_r)A.

questions.question: State Rayleigh's law of scattering. Red light has wavelength about 700 nm and blue about 400 nm; find the approximate ratio of scattered intensity of blue to red.
questions.answer: Rayleigh's law: for particles much smaller than the wavelength, scattered intensity I is proportional to 1/lambda^4. Ratio I_blue/I_red = (lambda_red/lambda_blue)^4 = (700/400)^4 = (1.75)^4 = about 9.4. So blue is scattered roughly 9 times more strongly than red.
questions.explanation: I proportional to 1/lambda^4; take the ratio.

questions.question: Why does the sky appear blue during the day but the Sun appears reddish at sunrise and sunset?
questions.answer: Air molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of light, so Rayleigh's law (I proportional to 1/lambda^4) applies. Short wavelengths (blue) are scattered far more than long ones, and this scattered blue light reaching the eye from all over the sky makes it look blue. At sunrise/sunset the Sun is near the horizon, so its light passes through a much longer atmospheric path; almost all the blue is scattered away and mainly the long-wavelength red/orange light reaches the observer, so the Sun looks reddish.
questions.explanation: Same 1/lambda^4 law; sky = scattered blue, red Sun = long path removes blue.

questions.question: Distinguish between a continuous spectrum and a line spectrum, giving one source of each.
questions.answer: A continuous spectrum is an unbroken band containing all wavelengths with colours merging into one another; it is produced by hot glowing solids, liquids or dense gases (e.g. an incandescent bulb filament). A line spectrum consists of sharp, bright, isolated lines on a dark background, each a definite wavelength; it is produced by excited atoms of a low-pressure gas (e.g. sodium vapour or a hydrogen discharge tube). A line spectrum is characteristic of the element.
questions.explanation: Nature + source of each type.

questions.question: Explain the formation of the primary rainbow. State the two optical processes involved, the approximate angle at which it is seen, and the colour order.
questions.answer: A primary rainbow forms when sunlight falls on raindrops with the Sun behind the observer. Two processes act inside each drop: (1) refraction, which bends the light on entry and exit and disperses it into colours because water's refractive index depends on wavelength; and (2) total internal reflection at the back of the drop. In the primary bow the light is refracted on entering, undergoes ONE total internal reflection, and is refracted again on leaving. The emergent light makes an angle of about 40 to 42 degrees with the incoming sunlight. Because violet is deviated slightly differently from red, the colours separate: RED appears on the OUTER (upper) edge of the bow and VIOLET on the INNER (lower) edge. The observer sees a coloured arc with the Sun behind them.
questions.explanation: One internal reflection, 40-42 deg, red outside.

questions.question: Describe the different types of emission spectra and explain what an absorption spectrum and Fraunhofer lines are.
questions.answer: Emission spectra come directly from a source and are of three kinds. (a) Continuous spectrum: an unbroken band of all wavelengths, emitted by hot solids, liquids or highly compressed hot gases (e.g. a bulb filament, molten metal). (b) Line spectrum: sharp bright isolated lines on a dark background, emitted by excited atoms of a low-pressure gas (e.g. sodium, hydrogen, neon); each element has its own line pattern, so it acts as a fingerprint. (c) Band spectrum: closely spaced lines forming bands, emitted by excited molecules (e.g. nitrogen). An ABSORPTION spectrum is formed when white light with a continuous spectrum passes through a cooler gas: the gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it would emit when hot, leaving a continuous spectrum crossed by DARK lines. In the solar spectrum these dark lines are the FRAUNHOFER LINES, produced by absorption in the Sun's cooler outer gases; matching them to known element lines reveals which elements are present in the Sun and stars.
questions.explanation: Three emission types + absorption + Fraunhofer lines.

questions.question: Why do clouds usually appear white while the clear sky appears blue?
questions.answer: The clear sky looks blue because air molecules, being much smaller than the wavelength of light, scatter short (blue) wavelengths far more than long ones (Rayleigh's law, I proportional to 1/lambda^4). Clouds, however, consist of relatively large water droplets whose size is comparable to or larger than the wavelength of light; for such large particles Rayleigh's law does not apply and all wavelengths are scattered almost equally. Since all colours are scattered by the same amount, the scattered light stays white, so clouds appear white.
questions.explanation: Small molecules -> blue (1/lambda^4); large droplets -> all colours equally -> white.

questions.question: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours by a prism is called:
questions.explanation: White light separating into colours is dispersion.

questions.question: The correct order of colours in the spectrum from least to most deviated is:
questions.explanation: Red deviates least, violet most, so least-to-most is Red to Violet.

questions.question: In a glass prism, which colour is deviated the most?
questions.explanation: Violet has the highest refractive index and is deviated most.

questions.question: Which colour is deviated the least by a prism?
questions.explanation: Red has the lowest refractive index and least deviation.

questions.question: Dispersion occurs because the refractive index of the medium depends on the:
questions.explanation: n varies with wavelength, causing different deviations.

questions.question: For ordinary glass, which relation between refractive indices is correct?
questions.explanation: Refractive index is larger for shorter (violet) wavelengths.

questions.question: The band of seven colours obtained on dispersion is called the:
questions.explanation: The coloured band is the spectrum.

questions.question: Which colour has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum?
questions.explanation: Violet has the shortest visible wavelength.

questions.question: The word VIBGYOR lists the spectral colours in order of:
questions.explanation: V (most deviated) to R (least deviated).

questions.question: Who first showed that white light is a mixture of colours?
questions.explanation: Newton demonstrated the composition of white light with a prism.

questions.question: White light passing through a prism forms a spectrum because different colours have different:
questions.explanation: Different speeds in glass mean different refractive indices and deviations.

questions.question: Dispersion of light does NOT occur in:
questions.explanation: In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed c, so no dispersion.

questions.question: For a thin prism, the deviation of a colour is given by delta =
questions.explanation: Thin-prism deviation is (n-1)A.

questions.question: If a thin prism has A = 5 degrees and n = 1.5 for a colour, its deviation is:
questions.explanation: delta = (1.5-1)(5) = 2.5 degrees.

questions.question: Two colours pass through the same thin prism. The one with larger refractive index has:
questions.explanation: delta = (n-1)A increases with n.

questions.question: In vacuum, red and violet light travel at:
questions.explanation: All colours share the speed c in vacuum, so no dispersion.

questions.question: A thin prism (A = 4 degrees) gives deviation 2 degrees for yellow. The refractive index for yellow is:
Dispersion is a property of the:
questions.explanation: Dispersion arises from the medium's wavelength-dependent n.

questions.question: The dispersive power of a prism is given by omega =
questions.explanation: omega = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1).

questions.question: Dispersive power of a prism depends on:
questions.explanation: omega is independent of A; it depends only on material.

questions.question: The unit of dispersive power is:
questions.explanation: omega is a ratio, hence unit-less.

questions.question: For a prism n_v = 1.66, n_r = 1.64, n_y = 1.65. Its dispersive power is about:
Angular dispersion produced by a thin prism equals:
questions.explanation: Angular dispersion = delta_v - delta_r = (n_v - n_r)A.

questions.question: A thin prism (A = 10 degrees) has n_v = 1.53, n_r = 1.51. The angular dispersion is:
Which glass generally has the higher dispersive power?
questions.explanation: Flint glass disperses more than crown glass.

questions.question: A combination that produces deviation without dispersion is called:

questions.question: The splitting of white light into its colours by a prism is called ____.

questions.explanation: Thin-prism deviation formula.

questions.question: The angular dispersion produced by a thin prism equals (n_violet - n_red) times ____.

questions.question: A hot glowing solid produces a ____ spectrum.
questions.explanation: Hot solids give continuous spectra.

questions.question: Excited atoms of a low-pressure gas give a ____ spectrum.
questions.explanation: Excited atoms emit line spectra.

questions.explanation: The collimator produces a parallel beam.

questions.explanation: Primary bow: one internal reflection.

questions.explanation: Red is on the outer edge of the primary bow.

questions.question: By Rayleigh's law, scattered intensity is proportional to 1 divided by lambda raised to the power ____.
questions.explanation: I is proportional to 1/lambda^4.

questions.question: The sky appears ____ because air molecules scatter short wavelengths most.
questions.explanation: Blue scatters most, so the sky looks blue.

questions.question: State what is meant by the spectrum of white light and name the seven colours in order.
questions.answer: The spectrum is the band of colours obtained when white light is dispersed by a prism. The seven colours, from most deviated to least, are Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR).
questions.explanation: Definition + VIBGYOR order.

questions.question: Explain why a prism disperses white light while a rectangular glass slab does not.
questions.answer: In both, each colour has a different refractive index, so in a slab too colours are refracted by different amounts. But in a parallel-sided slab the two surfaces are parallel, so the colours that separate on entry recombine on exit and the emergent beam is white (only laterally shifted). A prism has two non-parallel surfaces, so the deviations at the two faces add instead of cancelling, and the colours emerge separated as a visible spectrum.
questions.explanation: Slab surfaces are parallel (recombine); prism faces are inclined (deviations add).

questions.question: Why does dispersion occur in glass but not in vacuum?
questions.answer: In glass the refractive index (and hence the speed of light) depends on wavelength, so different colours are deviated by different amounts and separate. In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed c, so there is no wavelength-dependent deviation and no dispersion.
questions.explanation: n depends on lambda in glass; constant c in vacuum.

questions.question: A thin prism of angle 8 degrees is made of glass with n = 1.5 for yellow light. Find the deviation of yellow light.
questions.explanation: Apply delta = (n-1)A.

questions.question: A prism has n_violet = 1.523, n_red = 1.513 and n_yellow = 1.518. Calculate its dispersive power.
questions.explanation: Substitute into omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1).

questions.question: A thin prism (A = 5 degrees) has n_violet = 1.66 and n_red = 1.64. Find the angular dispersion.
questions.answer: Angular dispersion = (n_violet - n_red)A = (1.66 - 1.64) x 5 = 0.02 x 5 = 0.10 degrees.
questions.explanation: Apply (n_v - n_r)A.

questions.question: Explain the difference between an achromatic combination and a direct-vision prism.
questions.answer: An achromatic combination of two prisms (usually crown and flint glass) is arranged so that the net dispersion of the two prisms cancels while a net deviation remains - it deviates light without spreading colours, useful in lenses. A direct-vision prism combination is arranged the opposite way: the net deviation cancels while a net dispersion remains, so light is dispersed into a spectrum but the mean ray is not deviated - useful for viewing spectra straight ahead.
questions.explanation: Achromatic: deviation without dispersion; direct-vision: dispersion without deviation.

questions.question: Name the three types of emission spectra and state the source of each.
questions.answer: (1) Continuous spectrum - hot glowing solids, liquids or dense gases. (2) Line spectrum - excited atoms of a low-pressure gas. (3) Band spectrum - excited molecules.
questions.explanation: Three emission types with sources.

questions.question: How is an absorption spectrum formed? Give one example.
questions.answer: When white light having a continuous spectrum passes through a cooler gas or vapour, the gas absorbs exactly those wavelengths it would emit if it were hot. The transmitted light then shows a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines at the absorbed wavelengths - an absorption spectrum. Example: the solar spectrum, whose dark Fraunhofer lines arise from absorption by the Sun's cooler outer gases.
questions.explanation: Cooler gas absorbs its own wavelengths -> dark lines; example solar spectrum.

questions.question: Why is a line spectrum called the fingerprint of an element?
questions.answer: Each element, when its atoms are excited, emits a set of spectral lines at wavelengths that are unique to that element. No two elements have the same line pattern, so the line spectrum identifies the element just as a fingerprint identifies a person.
questions.explanation: Unique line pattern per element.

questions.question: State the four conditions required to obtain a pure spectrum.
questions.answer: (1) A narrow slit must be used as the source. (2) The light from the slit must be made parallel by a collimating lens before striking the prism. (3) The prism must be set at the position of minimum deviation. (4) A second lens must focus each parallel emergent beam to a sharp image on the screen.
questions.explanation: Narrow slit, parallel light, minimum deviation, focusing lens.

questions.question: What is Newton's disc and what does it demonstrate?
questions.answer: Newton's disc is a circular disc painted with the seven VIBGYOR colours in sectors. When spun rapidly it appears whitish because the eye cannot resolve the separate colours and blends them. It demonstrates that white light is a combination of the seven colours (recombination of the spectrum).
questions.explanation: Spinning colour disc looks white; shows recombination.

questions.question: Name the three main parts of a spectrometer and state the function of the collimator.
questions.answer: The three main parts are the collimator, the prism table, and the telescope. The collimator (a slit with a converging lens) produces a parallel beam of light from the slit to fall on the prism.
questions.explanation: Collimator, prism table, telescope; collimator makes parallel beam.

questions.question: Compare the primary and secondary rainbows in terms of number of reflections, angle, and colour order.
questions.answer: Primary rainbow: one total internal reflection inside the drop, seen at about 40-42 degrees, red on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge. Secondary rainbow: two total internal reflections, seen at about 50-54 degrees, fainter, with the colour order reversed (violet on the outer edge, red on the inner edge).
questions.explanation: Primary: 1 reflection, 40-42 deg, red out. Secondary: 2 reflections, 50-54 deg, red in.

questions.question: Why is the secondary rainbow fainter than the primary rainbow?
questions.answer: In the secondary rainbow the light undergoes two total internal reflections inside the drop instead of one. Some light escapes (is lost) at each reflection, so less light reaches the observer, making the secondary bow fainter.
questions.explanation: Extra reflection loses light.

questions.question: State Rayleigh's law and use it to find how many times more strongly light of 450 nm is scattered than light of 900 nm.
questions.answer: Rayleigh's law: for particles much smaller than the wavelength, scattered intensity I is proportional to 1/lambda^4. Ratio = (900/450)^4 = 2^4 = 16. So 450 nm light is scattered 16 times more strongly than 900 nm light.
questions.explanation: I proportional to 1/lambda^4; ratio (900/450)^4 = 16.

questions.question: What is the Tyndall effect? Give one everyday example.
questions.answer: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal or fine suspended particles, which makes the path of a light beam visible. Example: the visible beam of a torch or cinema projector in a smoky or dusty room.
questions.explanation: Scattering by colloid particles makes the beam visible; example smoky room beam.

questions.question: Why does Rayleigh's law not apply to scattering by large water droplets?
questions.answer: Rayleigh's law (I proportional to 1/lambda^4) holds only when the scattering particles are much smaller than the wavelength of light. Large water droplets are comparable to or larger than the wavelength, so this condition fails; instead all wavelengths are scattered almost equally (large-particle scattering).
questions.explanation: Rayleigh needs particles much smaller than lambda; large drops scatter all colours equally.

questions.question: Explain why the sky appears blue and why it appears black to an astronaut in space.
questions.answer: The sky appears blue because air molecules, being much smaller than the wavelength of light, scatter short (blue) wavelengths far more than long ones (Rayleigh's law), and this scattered blue light reaches the eye from all directions. In space there is no atmosphere and hence no scattering of sunlight, so no scattered light reaches the eye from the sky and it appears black.
questions.explanation: Air scatters blue most -> blue sky; no air in space -> no scattering -> black.

questions.question: Why are red lights used for danger and stop signals?
questions.answer: Red light has the longest wavelength in the visible range, so by Rayleigh's law it is scattered the least by fog, smoke and dust. It therefore travels farthest through a hazy atmosphere and can be seen clearly from a great distance, making it ideal for danger and stop signals.
questions.explanation: Red scatters least, penetrates haze, seen from far.

questions.question: Why does the Sun appear white at noon but red at sunset?
questions.answer: At noon the Sun is overhead and its light travels the shortest path through the atmosphere, so relatively little blue is scattered away and the Sun looks white. At sunset the Sun is near the horizon and its light travels a much longer atmospheric path; most of the blue is scattered away, leaving mainly red and orange to reach the eye, so the Sun looks red.
questions.explanation: Short path at noon (white); long path at sunset removes blue (red).

questions.question: What is the difference between a pure spectrum and an impure spectrum?
questions.answer: In a pure spectrum the different colours do not overlap - each colour occupies a distinct position and the spectral lines are sharp and clearly separated. In an impure spectrum neighbouring colours overlap, so the band looks smeared and the colours are not clearly distinguished. A pure spectrum requires a narrow slit, parallel incident light, minimum-deviation setting and a focusing lens.
questions.explanation: Pure: colours do not overlap (sharp); impure: colours overlap (smeared).

questions.question: Explain the dispersion of white light by a prism. Include the cause of dispersion and the order of colours.
questions.answer: When a narrow beam of white light enters a glass prism, each colour is refracted (bent) by a different amount and the light spreads into a band of colours called the spectrum. The colours, from least deviated to most deviated, are Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (VIBGYOR). The cause of dispersion is that the refractive index of the glass depends on the wavelength of light: n is larger for short wavelengths (violet) and smaller for long wavelengths (red), i.e. n_violet > n_red. Since the deviation of a thin prism is delta = (n-1)A, a larger n produces a larger deviation, so violet (highest n) bends the most and red (lowest n) the least. In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed c, so there is no dispersion; dispersion is a property of the material medium.
questions.explanation: Definition, VIBGYOR order, n depends on lambda, delta = (n-1)A, no dispersion in vacuum.

questions.question: Using the thin-prism deviation formula, explain how angular dispersion and dispersive power are defined and why omega is independent of the prism angle.
questions.answer: For a thin prism, each colour deviates by delta = (n-1)A, where n is that colour's refractive index and A the refracting angle. The violet ray deviates by delta_v = (n_v - 1)A and the red ray by delta_r = (n_r - 1)A. The ANGULAR DISPERSION is their difference: delta_v - delta_r = (n_v - n_r)A, which measures the total angular spread of the spectrum. The mean deviation (taking yellow as the mean colour) is delta_y = (n_y - 1)A. The DISPERSIVE POWER is the ratio omega = (delta_v - delta_r)/delta_y = (n_v - n_r)A / [(n_y - 1)A]. The refracting angle A cancels, giving omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1). Because A cancels out, omega depends only on the material (through its refractive indices) and not on the size or angle of the prism.
questions.explanation: Derive angular dispersion, mean deviation, ratio; A cancels so omega is material-only.

questions.question: A crown-glass prism has n_violet = 1.523, n_red = 1.513 and n_yellow = 1.517, with refracting angle A = 6 degrees. Find (a) the deviation of yellow light, (b) the angular dispersion, and (c) the dispersive power.
questions.answer: (a) Deviation of yellow: delta_y = (n_y - 1)A = (1.517 - 1) x 6 = 0.517 x 6 = 3.102 degrees. (b) Angular dispersion = (n_v - n_r)A = (1.523 - 1.513) x 6 = 0.010 x 6 = 0.060 degrees. (c) Dispersive power omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1) = 0.010/0.517 = 0.0193, or equivalently angular dispersion / mean deviation = 0.060/3.102 = 0.0193. So omega is about 0.019.

questions.question: Classify the different types of spectra with their sources and one example each.
questions.answer: Spectra are of two broad kinds: emission and absorption. EMISSION spectra: (a) Continuous - an unbroken band of all wavelengths, from hot solids, liquids or dense gases (example: incandescent bulb filament). (b) Line - sharp bright isolated lines from excited atoms of a low-pressure gas (example: sodium vapour lamp), unique to each element. (c) Band - closely spaced lines forming bands, from excited molecules (example: nitrogen). ABSORPTION spectrum: a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines, formed when white light passes through a cooler gas that absorbs its characteristic wavelengths (example: the solar spectrum with its Fraunhofer lines). Line spectra act as fingerprints identifying elements, and matching solar dark lines with element lines reveals the composition of the Sun and stars.
questions.explanation: Emission (continuous/line/band) + absorption, each with source and example.

questions.question: Describe the spectrometer: its main parts and how it is used to obtain a pure spectrum. Also state how the spectrum can be recombined into white light.
questions.answer: A spectrometer has three main parts. (1) The COLLIMATOR - a narrow slit with a converging lens that produces a parallel beam of light. (2) The PRISM TABLE - a rotatable platform carrying the prism, which can be set at the position of minimum deviation. (3) The TELESCOPE - which gathers the parallel emergent rays and focuses each colour to a sharp line, and can be rotated on a graduated circular scale to measure angles. To obtain a PURE spectrum the four conditions are met: a narrow slit, parallel incident light (collimator), minimum-deviation setting, and a focusing lens (in the telescope) - so the colours do not overlap. RECOMBINATION: dispersion is reversible. Placing a second identical but inverted prism after the first bends the colours back together to give white light; alternatively, a rapidly spinning Newton's disc (painted with VIBGYOR sectors) appears whitish because the eye blends the colours.
questions.explanation: Collimator/prism table/telescope; four conditions; recombination via inverted prism or Newton's disc.

questions.question: Explain in detail how a rainbow is formed, distinguishing the primary and secondary bows.
questions.answer: A rainbow is a natural spectrum formed by sunlight falling on raindrops, with the Sun behind the observer. Inside each drop two processes act: refraction (which also disperses the colours, since water's refractive index depends on wavelength) and total internal reflection. PRIMARY RAINBOW: sunlight enters the top of a drop, is refracted and dispersed, undergoes ONE total internal reflection at the back of the drop, and is refracted again on leaving. The emergent light makes about 40-42 degrees with the incoming sunlight. Red appears on the OUTER edge and violet on the INNER edge. SECONDARY RAINBOW: light entering the lower part of a drop undergoes TWO total internal reflections before emerging at about 50-54 degrees. It is fainter (light is lost at each reflection) and its colour order is REVERSED - red on the inner edge and violet on the outer edge. Thus dispersion plus total internal reflection in millions of raindrops produces the coloured arcs.
questions.explanation: Refraction + dispersion + TIR; primary (1 reflection, 40-42 deg, red out); secondary (2 reflections, 50-54 deg, red in, fainter).

questions.question: State Rayleigh's law of scattering, describe how scattering depends on particle size, and use the law to compare the scattering of violet (400 nm) and red (700 nm) light.
questions.answer: Rayleigh's law states that when the scattering particles are much smaller than the wavelength of light, the intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength: I is proportional to 1/lambda^4. Hence short wavelengths (violet, blue) are scattered much more strongly than long wavelengths (red). The law depends on particle size: it holds only for particles much smaller than lambda (such as air molecules); for particles comparable to or larger than lambda (such as cloud droplets) the scattering becomes almost independent of wavelength and all colours scatter nearly equally. Comparing violet and red: I_violet/I_red = (lambda_red/lambda_violet)^4 = (700/400)^4 = (1.75)^4 = about 9.4. So violet light is scattered roughly 9 times more strongly than red light.
questions.explanation: Law, size condition, and (700/400)^4 = about 9.4 for violet vs red.

questions.question: Using the idea of scattering, explain the blue colour of the sky, the red Sun at sunset, the white colour of clouds, and the use of red in danger signals.
questions.answer: All four phenomena follow from scattering and Rayleigh's law (I proportional to 1/lambda^4 for small particles). (1) BLUE SKY: air molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of light and scatter short (blue) wavelengths most; this scattered blue light reaches the eye from all directions, so the sky looks blue. (2) RED SUN AT SUNSET: near the horizon sunlight travels a long atmospheric path, so most of the blue is scattered away and mainly red and orange light reaches the observer directly, making the Sun look red. (3) WHITE CLOUDS: cloud droplets are large compared with the wavelength, so Rayleigh's law fails and all wavelengths are scattered almost equally; the scattered light stays white, so clouds look white. (4) RED DANGER SIGNALS: red has the longest wavelength and is scattered least, so it penetrates farthest through fog and haze and is visible from the greatest distance - ideal for danger and stop signals.
questions.explanation: Blue sky, red sunset, white clouds (large drops), red signals (least scattered).

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'A student directs a narrow beam of white light onto one face of a triangular glass prism in a dark room. On a screen beyond the prism she observes a band of colours ranging from red to violet.' (a) Name the phenomenon observed. (b) Which colour is nearest the base of the deviation and why? (c) Why does this not happen in vacuum? (d) Name the colours in order on the screen.
questions.answer: (a) The phenomenon is dispersion of white light. (b) Violet is deviated most (bent nearest the base of the prism) because glass has the highest refractive index for violet, and deviation increases with refractive index. (c) In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed c, so there is no wavelength-dependent deviation and no dispersion. (d) The colours in order are Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (VIBGYOR), with red deviated least and violet most.
questions.explanation: Dispersion; violet deviated most (highest n); no dispersion in vacuum; VIBGYOR order.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'A thin prism of refracting angle A = 6 degrees is made of glass for which n = 1.50 for yellow, 1.51 for violet and 1.49 for red.' (a) Find the deviation of yellow light. (b) Find the angular dispersion. (c) Why is A the same for all three colours? (d) Would the deviation increase or decrease if A were larger?
questions.answer: (a) delta_yellow = (n-1)A = (1.50-1) x 6 = 0.50 x 6 = 3 degrees. (b) Angular dispersion = (n_violet - n_red)A = (1.51-1.49) x 6 = 0.02 x 6 = 0.12 degrees. (c) A is the geometric refracting angle of the prism, a fixed property of its shape; it is the same for all colours because it does not depend on wavelength. (d) Since delta = (n-1)A, a larger A gives a larger deviation for every colour.
questions.explanation: (a) 3 deg, (b) 0.12 deg, (c) A is geometric, wavelength-independent, (d) increases with A.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'For a certain prism material, n_violet = 1.532, n_red = 1.514 and n_yellow = 1.523.' (a) Calculate the dispersive power. (b) Does the answer change if the refracting angle is doubled? (c) Which glass, crown or flint, would have a larger value of this quantity? (d) State the unit of dispersive power.
questions.answer: (a) omega = (n_violet - n_red)/(n_yellow - 1) = (1.532 - 1.514)/(1.523 - 1) = 0.018/0.523 = 0.0344, about 0.034. (b) No - dispersive power depends only on the material, not on the refracting angle, so doubling A leaves omega unchanged. (c) Flint glass has the larger dispersive power. (d) Dispersive power has no unit; it is a pure number.
questions.explanation: (a) 0.034, (b) unchanged, (c) flint glass, (d) no unit.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'In a physics lab, three light sources are examined through a spectroscope: an electric bulb filament, a sodium vapour lamp, and light from a nitrogen discharge that shows grouped lines.' (a) What type of spectrum does the bulb give? (b) What type does the sodium lamp give? (c) What type does the nitrogen source give and why? (d) Which of these can identify an element?
questions.answer: (a) The hot bulb filament gives a continuous spectrum (all wavelengths). (b) The sodium vapour lamp (excited atoms of a low-pressure gas) gives a line (emission) spectrum. (c) The nitrogen discharge gives a band spectrum, because the light comes from excited molecules, which produce groups of closely spaced lines forming bands. (d) The line spectrum (sodium) can identify an element, since each element has its own characteristic set of lines.
questions.explanation: Continuous (bulb), line (sodium), band (molecular nitrogen); line spectrum identifies element.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'When sunlight is examined with a spectroscope, a continuous coloured band is seen crossed by many fine dark lines.' (a) What are these dark lines called? (b) How are they produced? (c) What do they tell astronomers? (d) Name the instrument parts needed to see a pure spectrum.
questions.answer: (a) The dark lines are the Fraunhofer lines. (b) They are produced when the continuous light from the Sun's hot photosphere passes through the cooler gases of the Sun's outer atmosphere, which absorb their characteristic wavelengths, leaving dark lines. (c) By matching the dark lines with the known bright lines of elements, astronomers identify which elements are present in the Sun and stars. (d) A pure spectrum needs a narrow slit, a collimator (parallel beam), the prism at minimum deviation, and a focusing lens/telescope.
questions.explanation: Fraunhofer lines; absorption by cooler solar gases; reveal composition; slit+collimator+min deviation+telescope.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'After a rain shower, an observer facing away from the Sun sees a bright coloured arc, and above it a fainter second arc.' (a) Name the two arcs. (b) State the colour on the outer edge of each. (c) How many internal reflections form each? (d) Why is the upper arc fainter?
questions.answer: (a) The bright lower arc is the primary rainbow; the fainter upper arc is the secondary rainbow. (b) In the primary rainbow red is on the outer edge; in the secondary rainbow the order is reversed, so violet is on the outer edge (red inner). (c) The primary forms after one total internal reflection inside each drop; the secondary after two. (d) The secondary (upper) arc is fainter because light is lost at each internal reflection, and it undergoes an extra reflection, so less light reaches the observer.
questions.explanation: Primary/secondary; red outer (primary), violet outer (secondary); 1 vs 2 reflections; extra reflection loses light.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'A beam of white light passes through a medium containing very fine particles much smaller than the wavelength of light. The scattering follows Rayleigh's law.' (a) Write Rayleigh's law. (b) Which is scattered more, 450 nm or 650 nm light? (c) Find the ratio of their scattered intensities. (d) What would change if the particles were much larger than the wavelength?
questions.answer: (a) Rayleigh's law: I is proportional to 1/lambda^4 for particles much smaller than the wavelength. (b) The 450 nm light (shorter wavelength) is scattered more. (c) I_450/I_650 = (650/450)^4 = (1.444)^4 = about 4.35, so 450 nm is scattered roughly 4.3 times more. (d) For particles much larger than the wavelength, Rayleigh's law no longer applies; scattering becomes nearly independent of wavelength and all colours scatter almost equally.
questions.explanation: Law; 450 nm scatters more; ratio (650/450)^4 = about 4.3; large particles scatter all colours equally.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'A traveller notices that the midday sky is blue, the setting Sun is red, distant clouds are white, and railway stop signals are red.' (a) Why is the midday sky blue? (b) Why is the setting Sun red? (c) Why are the clouds white? (d) Why are stop signals red?
questions.answer: (a) Air molecules (much smaller than the wavelength) scatter short blue wavelengths most (Rayleigh's law), so scattered blue light from all directions makes the sky blue. (b) At sunset the light travels a long atmospheric path; most of the blue is scattered away, leaving red/orange to reach the eye, so the Sun looks red. (c) Cloud droplets are large compared with the wavelength, so they scatter all wavelengths almost equally and the scattered light stays white. (d) Red has the longest wavelength and is scattered least, so it penetrates haze and fog and is seen from farthest away, making it ideal for stop signals.
questions.explanation: Blue sky (small particles, 1/lambda^4); red Sun (long path); white clouds (large drops); red signals (least scattered).

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'In a dark room a beam from a projector is invisible until someone stirs up dust or lets in smoke, after which the beam path glows.' (a) Name the effect. (b) Why does the beam become visible? (c) What does this tell us about the particle size? (d) Give one more everyday example.
questions.answer: (a) This is the Tyndall effect. (b) The suspended dust or smoke particles scatter the light sideways towards the eye, so the path of the beam becomes visible. (c) The particles are small (colloidal-sized) suspended particles that scatter visible light; when very small, short wavelengths scatter most, sometimes giving a bluish tinge. (d) Another example: the visible beam of a torch or car headlights in fog, or sunlight streaming through a dusty window.
questions.explanation: Tyndall effect; particles scatter light to the eye; small suspended particles; example fog/headlight beam.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer. 'Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a prism and obtained a spectrum, then used a second prism to recombine the colours into white light.' (a) What did the first prism do? (b) What did the second prism do? (c) What did Newton conclude about white light? (d) Name a rotating device that shows the same recombination.
questions.answer: (a) The first prism dispersed the white sunlight into its spectrum of colours. (b) The second (inverted) prism recombined the separated colours back into white light. (c) Newton concluded that white light is not a single pure colour but a mixture of the seven spectral colours. (d) Newton's disc, a spinning disc painted with the VIBGYOR colours, appears whitish and demonstrates the same recombination.
questions.explanation: First prism disperses; second recombines; white light is a mixture; Newton's disc.
